Two of the three current problems (onboarding completion -4%, activation -6%) point at the same funnel stage, and the inherited record has two mutually reinforcing entries there: memory_86 (shortened onboarding lifted completion and time-to-value) and memory_31 (fewer required signup fields lifted first-week activation). That makes onboarding simplification the direction with the most convergent support and the best chance of moving both metrics with a single slot. I am deliberately not chasing the competitor with promotional_pricing: memory_73 records exactly that trade — 31% more signups and 18% more revenue but a 12-point early retention drop — which is the opposite of the sustainable qualified-revenue objective, so the competitive pressure is precisely the situation the memory warns against. Referral incentives (memory_57) are sound but target established customers and address neither declining metric; enterprise sales-assist (memory_44) is orthogonal to the SMB/self-serve funnel where the decline is.

I want to verify memory_86 because it is the load-bearing basis for the intended action and I need to see whether the original lift was in completion rate alone or actually carried through to retained, qualified accounts. I want to verify memory_91 as the strongest alternative use of the slot, since activation messaging targets the larger of the two declines directly and could beat onboarding work if its original effect was durable rather than a week-one engagement bump.

Risk to flag: 'simplification' can be achieved by removing qualification fields and steps, which may inflate completion and activation while degrading lead quality and downstream conversion — the same shape of failure as memory_73, just further up the funnel. The experiment must therefore be instrumented on retained qualified revenue and 30-day retention, not on completion rate alone, and should strip friction (steps, sequencing, defaults) before stripping any field that feeds qualification.

Uncertainty remaining: all six memories are consolidated summaries whose effect sizes, sample sizes, and durations are not stated, and the newest is 15 days old — conditions have shifted with the competitor launch, so prior lifts may not replicate. The QoQ declines may also be driven by the competitor changing traffic mix rather than by onboarding degradation, in which case fixing onboarding will underperform. I am running this at standard experiment scale with a holdout rather than a broad rollout, and will revisit if verification of memory_86 shows the original result was weak, short-horizon, or measured only on proxy metrics.
